name: Marketplace Quality and Liquidity

positioning.oneLineSummary: Tests whether both sides of a marketplace receive better value and whether local liquidity improves as participation grows.
positioning.productLabel: Marketplace Quality and Liquidity Lens — based on Bill Gurley's public writing
notAClaimOf: user growth proving a network effect

attribution.display: Based on Bill Gurley's public Above the Crowd marketplace writing

neutralParaphrase: Evaluate a marketplace through value improvement on both sides, demand and supply pull, local liquidity, fragmentation, onboarding friction, frequency, payment flow, technology/workflow value, and whether each additional participant improves later participants' experience.

locator.value: Lines 10-43 and factors 1-10: both-side pull, marketplace characteristics, liquidity, payment flow, and network effects
Section 2, lines 35-39: genuine network effects are rare and must improve incremental-user value

requiredConditions: Distinct participant sides and the transaction or interaction are defined.
Liquidity is measured in the relevant local geography, category, or cohort.
Network effects are separated from scale economies and marketing.

requiredEvidence.description: Experience and economic improvement versus the status quo for every material participant side.
Search-to-match, fill rate, time to match, failure rate, availability, repeat, and density by local market or segment.
Organic and paid acquisition, activation, retention, onboarding cost, concentration, and fragmentation on both sides.
Whether added participants causally improve price, selection, wait time, match quality, trust, or another user outcome.

decisionQuestions: What is materially better for each participant side?
Where is the marketplace liquid and where does it fail?
Does incremental supply attract demand and incremental demand attract supply?
Which side is structurally concentrated or expensive to onboard?
Does added participation improve later-user outcomes after controlling for spend and product changes?
positiveSignals: Both sides receive verified experience or economic value.
Liquidity improves within repeatable local units.
Growth becomes easier as density rises.
Payment or workflow integration strengthens value without trapping participants unfairly.
redFlags: The company reports total listings or users but not successful matches.
Only supply is aggregated; demand is purchased repeatedly.
Liquidity exists only in one subsidized micro-market.
A network effect is inferred from company size.
disconfirmingEvidence: High supplier-onboarding friction can later become a barrier if liquidity and retention are proven.
Low-frequency markets can work when transaction value and trust are high.
A concentrated side can still support a platform under strong contracts and value alignment.
A marketplace may create value without a strong network effect.
contraindications: Do not add the ten factors into a success-probability score.
Do not aggregate local liquidity into one global metric.
Do not call scale economy or brand a network effect.

instructions: Define sides, interaction, and local liquidity unit.
Measure side value, activation, matches, failures, retention, and density.
Test whether added participation improves later-user outcomes.
Review fragmentation, onboarding, frequency, payment, and concentration.
Conclude compounding marketplace, emerging local liquidity, subsidized or one-sided, non-marketplace aggregation, or insufficient.

deterministicRule.serviceBoundary: Liquidity, fill rate, density, retention, concentration, and network-effect tests must be computed outside the language model.

sourceReliability.high: Reconciled local transaction data plus participant and causal evidence.

evidenceStrength.high: Added participation repeatedly improves both-side outcomes.

evidenceCoverage.high: Value, liquidity, growth, fragmentation, frequency, payment, network causality, and counterevidence covered.

applicabilityConfidence.high: Marketplace dynamics determine growth and defensibility.

judgmentConfidence.high: Repeated local and causal evidence supports the conclusion.

empiricalQualifications: Marketplace dynamics are local and path-dependent.
Execution and policy can dominate structural attractiveness.

rights.notes: Public author material is neutrally paraphrased; the factor list is not copied as a scorecard.

openIssues: Define causal network-effect and local-liquidity review protocol.
